summary: Alabama's state amphibian, a large burrowing salamander that lives nowhere else on earth.
description: A large, dark brown salamander about 8 inches long, with no markings, a long body, and short legs.  It has no lungs and breathes through its moist skin.
habitat: Mature hardwood forest with a closed canopy, on steep slopes and in moist ravines, where ledges of limestone lie over siltstone that holds water.  It lives in small burrows and cracks in that rock.
life: It lives about ten years and breeds slowly, laying 6 to 10 eggs in its burrow.  The young hatch as small salamanders, with no stage in the water.
alabama: Its whole range is about 60,000 acres of the Red Hills, between the Alabama River on the west and the Conecuh River on the east, in Butler, Conecuh, Covington, Crenshaw, Monroe, and Wilcox Counties.
threats: The Service's profile does not list threats.  The salamander's small range, slow breeding, and need for mature, shaded forest leave it little margin.
notes: The Encyclopedia of Alabama notes that it was the first amphibian in North America to receive federal protection.

summary: A large salamander that keeps its gills for life, found only in the streams of the upper Black Warrior basin.
description: A large aquatic salamander up to 9.5 inches long, with a flattened head and body, feathery gills on the outside, and four toes on each foot.  It is usually brown, sometimes spotted, with a dark stripe through the eye.
habitat: Medium and large streams with bottoms of clay or bedrock and little sand, and with rock crevices and slabs for shelter and for laying eggs.
alabama: Found only in Alabama, in streams above the Fall Line in the Black Warrior River basin.  It is known from 14 scattered sites in the Sipsey Fork, Locust Fork, Mulberry Fork, North River, and their tributaries, in Blount, Tuscaloosa, Walker, and Winston Counties.
threats: Silt, above all.  Heavy siltation fills the crevices it shelters in, cuts its food, and smothers its nests and eggs.

summary: The largest salamander in North America, a stream dweller of north Alabama proposed for listing as endangered.
description: A salamander up to two feet long, with a flattened body, a keeled tail, tiny eyes, and loose folds of skin along its sides, through which it breathes.
habitat: Cool, clear streams and rivers that flow all year.  Adults shelter under large flat rocks, and the young hide under smaller rocks and in gravel.
life: The male makes a nest under a rock, guards the eggs, and may stay on to guard the hatchlings.
alabama: The Service places northern Alabama within its range of 15 states.  The sources read for this entry do not name the streams.
range: Fifteen states, from New York to northern Alabama and Mississippi, with a separate population in Missouri
threats: Silt in streams, poor water quality, loss of habitat, disease, and collecting for the pet trade.  Of 626 populations on record, 41 percent are believed gone, and most of the rest are declining.
notes: The Missouri population was listed as endangered in 2021.  The Service proposed listing the eastern hellbender throughout its range on December 13, 2024.  No final rule has followed, so Alabama's hellbenders have no protection under the Act today.

summary: A slender, net-patterned salamander of the longleaf flatwoods, last seen in Alabama in 1981.
description: A slender salamander, black to chocolate-black, with a net of light gray markings.
habitat: Longleaf pine flatwoods and savannas.  It breeds in seasonal wetlands there and spends most of its life in the uplands nearby.
alabama: Alabama has old records from Mobile, Baldwin, Covington, and Houston Counties.  The last sighting in the state was in 1981, and the salamander is no longer known here.
countiesText: None today; once Mobile, Baldwin, Covington, and Houston
range: Santa Rosa and Okaloosa Counties in Florida, and Miller County in Georgia
threats: The loss of fire, which lets the flatwoods and their breeding ponds grow over, along with loss of habitat, predatory fish, fire ants, disease, drought, and a rising sea.

summary: A stout, warty frog of the longleaf pinelands, recorded in Alabama only once, in 1922.
description: A plump frog with a large head and a warty back, 2.2 to 4.1 inches long.  Its color runs from nearly black to brown, with reddish spots.  The females are the larger.
habitat: Longleaf pine uplands.  It breeds in isolated seasonal ponds that hold no predatory fish.
alabama: Alabama's only record is a sighting of three frogs near Mobile Bay, in Mobile County, in 1922.  No breeding pond has ever been found in the state.
range: Mississippi only, where a handful of populations survive
threats: Loss and breaking up of the pinelands, changes to the water in its breeding ponds, disease, predators, and the small size of the populations that remain.
